summary: This draft standard defines MIB objects for managing Ethernet-like interfaces, so management tools can monitor things such as errors and statistics on those links. It was replaced by RFC 1623.

plainLanguage.summary: Network managers need to peek at how an Ethernet connection is doing. This paper creates a standard list of things they can check, like how many mistakes happened.

subtitle: Counters and diagnostics for monitoring Ethernet interfaces

tldr.problem: Network operators need a standard way to monitor error rates, collisions and other statistics on Ethernet interfaces across different hardware.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1398 defines MIB objects that count frame errors, transmission collisions, alignment problems, and other Ethernet-specific events, plus diagnostic tests and hardware chipset identifiers.
tldr.outcome: Operators can now monitor Ethernet quality uniformly. This RFC was quickly replaced by RFC 1623, which extended the definitions.

today: RFC 1398 is obsoleted by RFC 1623, which expanded the Ethernet MIB. The objects remain the foundation for monitoring Ethernet interfaces in networks today.

sections.title: Ethernet Interface Monitoring
sections.content:
RFC 1398 defines the Management Information Base (MIB) objects for Ethernet and Ethernet-like interfaces such as IEEE 802.3, ISO 8802/3 and StarLAN. It allows operators to monitor and diagnose problems on these interfaces using SNMP. The RFC is based on the IEEE 802.3 Layer Management Specification and includes error counters, collision statistics, diagnostic tests, and identifiers for common Ethernet MAC hardware chips.

The RFC replaces RFC 1284 and was itself replaced by RFC 1623. Unlike the base Internet MIB which counts all octets and frames, this RFC focuses on Ethernet-specific events: what kinds of errors occur, how often collisions happen, and whether the hardware is working.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a standard way to ask an Ethernet port: how many messages were mangled, how many times did two senders bump into each other, what is the hardware inside you. Every port answers with counters.

sections.title: Statistics and Error Counters
sections.content:
The Ethernet-like Statistics Group defines a set of read-only counters for each interface. Alignment errors count frames that are not an integral number of octets and fail the frame check sequence (FCS). FCS errors count frames of correct length that fail the checksum. Single and multiple collision frames track how many times a transmission was delayed by one collision versus more than one. Carrier sense errors count attempts to transmit when the medium was not clear. Deferred transmissions count frames held back because the medium was busy. Late collisions are collisions detected more than 512 bit-times (51.2 microseconds) into transmission, which indicate a cable fault or loop. Excessive collisions count frames that could not be sent due to too many collisions. Frame too long counts oversized received frames.

The Ethernet-like Collision Statistics Group is optional and provides a histogram: for each possible number of collisions from 1 to 16, it counts how many frames experienced exactly that many collisions on transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: The counters tell the story of what went wrong: scrambled, wrong checksum, collisions with one neighbor, collisions with many, cable fault, too long, internal hardware error. Each counter is a tally mark on the Ethernet port.

sections.title: Tests and Hardware Identification
sections.content:
The RFC defines diagnostic tests that an operator can run on an Ethernet interface. A loopback test configures the MAC chip to run an internal loopback, checking its memory and logic without sending anything on the wire. The test can only run when the interface is offline. The Time-Domain Reflectometry (TDR) test is available on most Ethernet types except 10BaseT and 10BaseF and helps locate a cable fault by measuring how long it takes to detect a collision or loss of carrier. The result is measured in 100-nanosecond units, so a result helps estimate the distance to the fault.

The RFC also names common Ethernet MAC chipsets for identification: AMD 7990 and 79900, Intel 82586 and 82596, Seequences 8003, National 8390 and SONIC, and Fujitsu 86950 and 86960. This allows management tools and operators to know what hardware is in use.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell Ethernet to run a self-check: send data around in a circle inside the chip, or ping the cable to find where it is broken. You can also ask the port what chip brand is inside it: is it Intel, AMD, or something else.

sections.title: Relationship to IEEE 802.3 and Extensibility
sections.content:
The MIB objects are grounded in the IEEE 802.3 Layer Management Specification. Rather than redefine Ethernet behavior, the RFC points to the IEEE specification, which describes in detail when and how to measure each attribute and what effects various MAC actions have. The RFC avoids duplicating information that is already available in the Internet-standard MIB or Generic Interface Extensions MIB, such as octet and frame counts, promiscuous mode status, and MAC addresses.

The MIB is designed to be extended. Each Ethernet-like interface type (ethernet-csmacd, iso88023-csmacd, starLan) is identified by specific ifType values in the MIB-II interface table, and they share the same set of objects defined here. Vendors can define additional objects for their own hardware in the registration tree delegated to enterprises. This structure allows the MIB to cover Ethernet variants without becoming unwieldy.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB matches what the IEEE standard actually measures. It does not try to be a complete list of everything; it fills in the gaps that other standards left. Vendors can add their own counters if they want, in their own part of the family tree.
